Copper has high resistance to electromigration and excellent thermal and electrical conductivity, so it is the main metal material for electrical interconnects,<sup>7–17</sup> as shown in Fig. 1. However, with the rapid development of integrated circuit industry, the wiring density and metal layer stacking continually increase, e.g., the length of the chip internal metal wiring has been up to tens of kilometers, and the number of the metal wiring layers is up to 15. The improvement in energy consumption and performance requires the size of transistors and metal interconnects to shrink continuously, with the resulting size efects. The more significant grain boundary scattering and interface scattering of electrons inside the metal caused by size efects are shown in Fig. 2.<sup>13</sup> When the width of copper interconnects line decreases, the current load increases sharply, then the resistivity increases sharply, which will damage the chip performance due to the serious resistance and capacitance delay and a large amount of Joule heat. Therefore, copper interconnects have been unable to meet the development needs of advanced integrated circuit in the post-Moore era, and it is urgent to find next-generation metal interconnect materials.

The electron mean free path of copper is 39 nm.<sup>18</sup> Generally, the larger the electron mean free path of the bulk metal, the lower the resistivity of the metal. When the characteristic size of interconnects is reduced to the electron mean free path of copper, the electrons inside the copper are subjected to strong grain boundary scattering and interface scattering, causing a sudden increase in resistivity. Compared with copper, cobalt has a smaller electron mean free path (about 10 nm);<sup>18</sup> that is, cobalt possesses a smaller size efect than copper.<sup>19</sup> When the trench critical dimension is above about 7 nm, copper wires have lower resistivity. When the trench critical dimension is below about 7 nm, cobalt wires exhibit even lower resistivity.<sup>20</sup> The resistivities of diferent widths for Cu and Co are shown in Fig. 3. In addition, in copper interconnects, the TiN barrier layer and copper seed layer with about 2 nm thickness in total are needed to prevent the interdifusion of copper and dielectric ${ \mathrm { S i } } / { \mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 } } ,$ which further reduces the width of copper interconnect line, resulting in a higher resistivity. Cobalt itself can act as a barrier layer or seed layer.<sup>21</sup> Theoretically, using cobalt as interconnect metal does not require a barrier layer and a seed layer with higher resistivity, thereby further improving the conductivity of the interconnect metal. Although cobalt has better electromigration resistance than copper, in practice, if a barrier layer is not used, cobalt will still difuse into the $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ dielectric layer or porous low-K dielectric layer.<sup>22</sup> In the absence of an seed layer or barrier layer, cobalt will also difuse into the trench of other layers along the interface of the filling layer/dielectric layer.<sup>23</sup> Cobalt is an ideal next-generation interconnected metal material to replace copper.

Rigsby et al.<sup>39</sup> found that $\mathrm { H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { B O } _ { 3 }$ could refine grain and reduce coating roughness, as shown in Fig. 6. Furthermore, when the content of ${ \mathrm { H } } _ { 3 } { \mathrm { B O } } _ { 3 }$ was too low, the trenches were sealed in advance, leaving many holes and gaps, as displayed in Fig. 7. The $\mathrm { H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { B O } _ { 3 }$ plays a relatively complex role in cobalt electroplating interconnects. During the cobalt electroplat ing process, due to the continuous occurrence of the hydrogen evolution reaction, the pH value of the local electrolyte near the cathode surface increases significantly. The $\mathrm { H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { B O } _ { 3 }$ must be converted into polyborates and the released $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ ions will reduce the local pH value and hinder the formation of ${ \mathrm { C o } } ( \mathrm { O H } ) _ { 2 }$ near the cathode surface.<sup>40</sup> In addition, polyborates are easily adsorbed on the cathode surface, occupying active sites for atomic hydrogen electro-reduction and inhibiting the hydrogen evolution reaction.<sup>41</sup> Generally, most chemical substances are adsorbed on the electrode surface, which can inhibit the electrodeposition of metal ions. However, as the concentration of $\mathrm { H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { B O } _ { 3 }$ increases, the adsorbed polyborate results in an increase in the current utilization rate of cobalt electrodeposition.<sup>39</sup> That is to say, the mechanism of converting $\mathrm { H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { B O } _ { 3 }$ into polyborates on the cathode surface, the mechanism of inhibiting the reduction of atomic hydrogen, the types of polyborates adsorbed on the cathode surface and their adsorption modes, and the mechanism of polyborates capturing metal ions to form complexes to improve current utilization are currently inconclusive. Research on $\mathrm { H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { B O } _ { 3 }$ in cobalt electroplating interconnects is still in its preliminary stage and there is room for discussion on the mechanism, but what is certain is that $\mathrm { H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { B O } _ { 3 }$ plays an indispensable role in cobalt electroplating from three aspects: stabilizing the pH, inhibiting surface hydrogen evolution, and promoting cobalt electrodeposition for high current utilization.

Dye additives are usually nitrogen-containing compounds, which are often regarded as levelers and applied to copper electroplating interconnects.<sup>45–54</sup> Dye additives have the characteristics of inhibiting metal electrodeposition and difusion dependence, so they can also be used for cobalt electroplating interconnects. Nitrotetrazolyl blue (NBT) and malachite green (MG) are the typical dye-type additives for cobalt electroplating, and their corresponding structures are shown in Fig. 10a. Li et al.<sup>31</sup> showed that NBT has a concentration gradient in the trench structure. As cobalt electrodeposition proceeds, the NBT content at the bottom of the trench is lower than that at the mouth, and therefore cobalt can be filled from bottom to top. Figure 10b shows the proposed difusion-dependent mechanism for cobalt bottom-up superfilling based on the NBT action mechanism. It is worth noting that, unlike copper electroplating, the bottom-up superfilling mechanism of cobalt electroplating is also related to the atomic hydrogen concentration on the electrode surface in addition to the type of additives. Some dye additives can promote the occurrence of the hydrogen evolution reaction, which afects the bottom-up superfilling efect by changing the cobalt electrodeposition current eficiency. Ma et al.<sup>55</sup> believed that MG can promote the generation of atomic hydrogen. There was a concentration gradient of MG in the trench, and the MG concentration was high at the trench mouth. At the same time, MG promoted the occurrence of the hydrogen evolution reaction at the trench mouth, resulting in a decrease in the current eficiency of cobalt electrodeposition there. In contrast, the current eficiency of cobalt electrodeposition at the bottom of the trench was high. Therefore, cobalt was densely superfilled from bottom to top. Based on this characteristic, an induction–dif fusion–adsorption mechanism suitable for cobalt bottom-up superfilling was proposed, as shown in Fig. 10c.

Another mechanism that is not afected by the types of additives is the hydrogen reduction-induced deactivation (HID) mechanism. Wu et al.<sup>59,60</sup> verified that the change of pH value afected the inhibiting ability of additives through cyclic voltammetry. During the cobalt electrodeposition process, a large amount of atomic hydrogen accumulates at the bottom of the via due to the large surface-to-volume ratio, and the inhibitor at the bottom of via is continuously protonated and loses the ability to inhibit the electro-reduction of cobalt ions. A schematic of the HID mechanism is presented in Fig. 12. According to the principles described in this mechanism, any additive that undergoes a transition between an inactive state and active state under the influence of hydrogen ions can control and achieve the cobalt bottomup superfilling.

surface_text: All electrochemical tests, including CV, LSV, and GMs, were performed in a three-electrode system connected to an electrochemical workstation (CHI660C). The working electrode is a platinum rotating disk electrode (Pt-RDE) with a diameter of 5 mm, and the counter electrode (CE) is a platinum wire electrode (Shanghai Raymagnetic Instruments Co., Ltd.), the reference electrode (RE) is a saturated mercurous sulfate electrode (Hg/Hg₂SO₄) (Shanghai Leimagnetic Instruments Co., Ltd.) . In the electrochemical tests, the velocity of the working electrode was adjusted to 1600 rpm and 100 rpm to simulate strong and weak convection in the blind hole, respectively [21]. In the voltage range from 0 to −1.6 V, the cyclic voltammetry is scanned, the scanning speed is 0.01 $\mathrm { V } / s ,$ scanning 2 segments. At a scan rate of 0.02 V/s, the LSV are scanned from $ { 0 \ \mathrm { t o } } - 1 . 6 \  { \mathrm { V } }$ . The constant current measurement requires pre-plating for 300 s at 1000 rpm. at a voltage of −0.15 V to deposit a cobalt layer on the working electrode at a set current density of 1 $. \mathrm { \bf A } / \mathrm { d m } ^ { 2 }$ . Then accelerator (MPS) and leveling agent (HMTA) were added to the basic plating bath for determination.

CV was used to analyze the inhibitory effect of HMTA molecule concentration on cobalt metal deposition at two different rotational speeds where the 100 rpm is used to simulate the weak convection at the bottom of the blind hole and the 1600 rpm is used to simulate the strong convection at the orifice area of the blind hole to evaluate the suppression efficiency under different mass transfer conditions and the CV results are shown in Fig. 1 and the corresponding absolute areas of dissolution peaks obtained from the CV curves is summarized. It can be seen Fig. 1 that the addition of HMTA leads to a decrease in the dissolution peak of cobalt at the low and high speeds, indicating that HMTA has an inhibitory effect on cobalt electrodeposition. Furthermore, as the concentration of HMTA increases from 1 ppm to 13 ppm, the dissolution peak of cobalt continues to decrease, indicating that the inhibitory ability of adding high concentrations of HMTA on cobalt deposition will become greater. But it is worth emphasizing that although the CV results indicate that the inhibitory ability of HMTA on cobalt deposition continues to increase with increasing concentration, it was found through the Hall cell experiments that the quality of the cobalt coating decreases when the concentration exceeds 13 ppm. Therefore, based on the results of CV and Hall cell experiments, the optimal concentration of HMTA was determined to be 13 ppm. Furthermore, the dissolution peak of the CV curve obtained at the high speed is significantly lower than that at the low speed, indicating that cobalt electrodeposition in the blind hole orifice area is more inhibited compared to the bottom area of the blind hole.

LSV was used to further analyze the inhibitory effect of HMTA molecule concentration on cobalt metal deposition at two different rotational speeds and the corresponding results are shown in Fig. 2. It can be seen from Fig. 2 that the reduction potential of cobalt attained from the electrolytes with the MPS was significantly shifted towards the positive potential direction compared to that form the base solution, which indicates that the addition of MPS accelerates the reduction process of cobalt ion. However, the addition of HMTA leads to a significant negative shift in the deposition potential of cobalt. Furthermore, at the same polarization potential, the deposition current density of cobalt obtained in the electrolyte with added HMTA was significantly lower than that in the base solution, indicating that The HMTA has a significant inhibitory effect on the reduction of cobalt. As the amount of HMTA increases, the negative shift of cobalt reduction potential and the decrease in reduction current density become greater, with the addition of 13 ppm HMTA providing the best inhibitory ability for cobalt deposition. In addition, it can also be clearly seen that the HMTA has a stronger inhibitory ability on cobalt deposition at high speeds than at the low speeds, which is consistent with the results of CV analysis. The re sults from CV and LSV indicate that the HMTA molecules as leveling agent can effectively enhance cathodic polarization and inhibit cobalt deposition, especially in the blind hole region of strong convection.

In this work, we propose a data-driven method to identify novel, high-efficiency, and environmentally friendly nitrogen-containing molecules as inhibitors for cobalt interconnections (Fig. 1). The computational details are described in the Methods section. We employed a DFT computational database to construct machine learning models. The molecular descriptors were calculated based on SMILES [39] (Simplified Molecular-Input Line-Entry System) strings. They were further filtered through a three-step dimensionality reduction workflow. Six machine learning models were systematically compared. XGBoost achieved the best R<sup>2</sup> and MAE after Bayesian hyperparameter optimization. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) [40] analysis was applied to quantitatively evaluate each descriptor's contribution to ΔE predictions. Crucially, these feature analysis insights were translated into chemical implications. ML models were employed for high-throughput screening of a commercial molecular library, from which three promising addi tives were identified. Electrochemical measurements demonstrated the surface polarization capability of the additives. Moreover, their application enabled electrodeposited cobalt films with precisely controlled nanoscale roughness. Furthermore, defect-free superfilling of TSVs was successfully achieved. This informatics framework presents an innovative approach to additive discovery while providing practical solutions for advanced cobalt metallization.

Through‑silicon via (TSV) technology is widely used in advanced packaging to achieve high-density interconnections (Fig. 8a). During the TSV filling process, the tip effect induced by the geometric structure results in enhanced electric field intensity and accelerated mass trans port at the top of the TSV [65], leading to the formation of voids or seam defects in VMS, as illustrated in Fig. S3. In contrast, cobalt superfilling i successfully achieved using 20 ppm APZ, 10 ppm MIDCN, and 50 ppm AEP, respectively (Fig. 8c–e). EDS mapping confirms the uniform deposition of cobalt throughout the entire via structure (Fig. 8f–h). Specifically, the purple region clearly illustrates the distribution of Co, while the yellow region serves as a structural reference, corresponding to the elemental mapping of the silicon substrate. This consistent and homogeneous distribution of Co demonstrates the effectiveness of these candidates as additives in achieving uniform and void-free Co deposition in high-aspect-ratio microstructures. The underlying bottom-up filling mechanism can be described as follows (Fig. 8b). In the initial stage of electrodeposition, additives uniformly adsorb onto the cobalt surface. As the deposition proceeds, the additive molecules within the TSV trenches are gradually depleted. Owing to mass transport constraints, the replenishment of additives inside the deep vias occurs at a slower rate than on the upper surface, resulting in a reduced inhibitor concentration within the trenches compared to the via opening. This concentration gradient leads to weaker suppression at the bottom of the via relative to its top. Consequently, the deposition rate is elevated at the bottom in comparison to the top, facilitating bottom-up filling and thereby enabling the formation of void-free interconnect structures.

What’s more, voltammetry curves were used to further study the influence of MG on HER without Co ion in the bath. The process of hydrogen evolution was significantly accelerated even though 2 ppm MG added into plating bath. The accelerating effect on HER can be enhanced with the increase of MG concentration. The MG could absorb on the cathode surface as active sites to promote the HER, which is consistent with EQCM analysis (Fig. 3). It should be noted that the current density obtained in EQCM analysis is slightly different from that of cyclic voltammetry analysis, which is due to the fact that rotation electrode was applied in cyclic voltammetry tests while there was none convection in EQCM test.

The surface morphology of cobalt deposit.—The surface morphology was analyzed to verify the acceleration of MG on HER, as shown in Figs. 6 and S5. Meanwhile, the MG act as the accelerator for hydrogen evolution which make hydrogen bubble increase and overflow from the coating surface. Electroplating.—The electroplating test was carried out in order to observe the influence of MG and pH on the bottom-up growth of cobalt. The test condition in filling experiments was the same as that in electroanalytical experiments except for stirring way. The ohmic losses difference caused by different stirring way can be neglected (Fig. S8). Electroplating test were investigated at the potential range of −1.19 V and −1.22 V since superconformal electrodeposition could be achieved due to intense pH and strong inhibition of MG. As shown in Fig. 7, there is almost no cobalt reduced when the cathode potential is −1.19 V. Referring to the previous voltammetry curve, when the external potential at −1.19 V, the main electrochemical reaction in the via is hydrogen ion reduction. When the deposition potential is −1.20 V, it can be seen that the deposition layer begins to appear at the bottom and side wall. According to Moffat’s description of the metal filling process in TSV,<sup>28,50,51</sup> the blocking effect caused by the coverage of inhibitors on the electrode makes the deposition efficiency of metal on the sidewall higher than that on the surface, which can form a passive-active transition. From the Fig. 7(b), it can be seen that the rapid deposition rates take place in the lower portion of the via, while the sidewall and outside surface remain in the passive state. What’s more, the boundary of the passive-active transition gradually rises at more positive potential in Fig. 7(c). The transition forms mainly due to the difference of the vias coverage caused by the breakdown and diffusion-limited process of the MG.<sup>28,52</sup>

Although boric acid is added to the bath as buffer, it can be seen from the Fig. 5 that the deposition efficiency of the same pH value at different rotational speeds is significantly different, especially at a lower pH value. Next, the filling conditions of cobalt metal under different pH values were studied, as shown in Fig. 8. When the bath was adjusted the pH to 3 by dilute sulfuric acid, almost nothing is deposited in the feature, as shown in Fig. 8(a). This indicates that the reaction occurring at this condition is mainly the reduction of H<sup>+</sup>, and the absorption of MG makes no cobalt deposit in the feature. After the pH value of the bath was up to 3.5, thin film was deposited on the central bottom rather than the bottom corners of the feature, as shown in Fig. 8(b). This model of deposition appears to differ from the higher deposition rate on the sidewall, which is based on the passive-active transition model. In other words, the MG inhibition effect still exist in the feature, and the cobalt deposit at the central bottom may be caused by some accelerant. In the absence of MG images (Fig. S10), the thickness of Co deposit in the feature, such as the bottom and the surrounding field, is nearly the same as that on the surface. Therefore, the local accelerant was probably regard as the formation of $\mathrm { C o O H ^ { + } _ { a d s } }$ at the bottom,<sup>53</sup> which caused by the rising in pH, rather than the breakdown of the MG. A local pH increases owing to hydrogen ion consumption and mass transport limitations,<sup>37</sup> especially when MG is adsorbed at the bottom.

The formation of local pH gradient is a process of time accumulation because the mass transport of proton is faster than that of suppressor. The coupling of MG depletion effects in feature filling with the local increasing pH could provide the explanation for the subsequent shift from the passive to active zone at the bottom. When different rotation speeds and concentration are applied at −1.20 V, the filling of metal Co was completely different, as shown in Fig. S11. The phenomenon of conformal deposition at 0 rpm indicates the conformal growth of cobalt since effective MG concentration gradient was not established. As the convection intensifies, there is no cobalt deposit on the outer surface and sidewall of the via since effective MG concentration gradient based on diffusion-limited within the feature was established.<sup>54</sup>The passive-active profile should be steady-state in nature, which is reflected in the potential-dependent incorporation balanced by the suppressor depletion gradient in the deposit.<sup>52</sup> However, this transition state gradually expands over time [Fig. 9(c)], which may be due to the disruption of inhibition caused by pH evolution, which is related to time evolution. After the stable passive-active transition zone is completed, the bottom-up growth process proceeds smoothly as shown in Figs. 9(d) and 9(e).

At the initial state, the cathode surface covered with inhibitor MG which suppress the Co reduction and promote the HER. During the electrodeposition, the deposit suppression gradient was formed because of the diffusion-limited of MG. The passive-active transition zone come into being, and then the zone grows until it covers the entire trench due to the induction HER of MG. Meantime, the effective pH gradient is also established due to the mass transport limitation of hydrogen ion, resulting that the current efficiency at the bottom is higher, as shown in stage b in Fig. 10. Compared with the formation of inhibition gradient, the disruption of MG caused by HER is weaker, which is more conducive to the bottom-up superfilling process. In summary, the induction-diffusion-adsorption mechanism, namely diffusion-adsorption effect caused by MG gradient and pH gradient as well as induction effect of MG on HER, was proposed to illustrate the bottom-up growth of cobalt.

According to this table, the extension of the lifetime and reduction in the scaling factor of Co by W alloying correlate closely with the improvement of surface and nanomechanical properties of the thin films. Notably, surface energy is an important thermodynamic factor that decides the wettability of a condensed matter to a heterogeneous supporting substrate. The deposited film with a lower surface energy would have a higher wetting tendency and thus should be with a greater substrate adherence than the counterpart with a higher surface energy. Indeed, the adhesion strength of the Co films after adding 0.03 at.% and 0.06 at.% of W is increased from 35.8 to 43.4 and 56.1 MPa, respectively, concurring well with the respective decrease in the surface energy from 70 to 66 and 60 mJ $\mathrm { m } ^ { - 2 }$ for CoW and $\mathrm { C o W } _ { \mathrm { m } } .$ As the added W is further increased to 0.11 at.%, the adhesion strength of the related $\mathrm { C o W _ { h } }$ film is reduced to 52.7 MPa, associated with an increase in the surface energy to 69 mJ $\mathbf { m } ^ { - 2 }$ . The measured data of $\mathrm { C o W _ { l } }$ and $\mathrm { C o W _ { h } }$ (high tungsten content) obviously deviates from the inverse variation trend for $\mathbf { C o } ,$ , CoW<sub>l</sub> and $\mathrm { C o W } _ { \mathrm { m } } .$ This deviation can be attributed to the strong affinity of W for oxygen [41], which likely results in a higher sticking coefficient of W atoms on the SiO₂ substrate compared to Co atoms [42]. This interfacial reaction likely facilitates the formation of tungsten oxide between the $\mathrm { C o W _ { h } }$ and $S \mathrm { i O _ { 2 } , }$ thereby enhancing adhesion strength. Such behavior has also been reported in Co-Zr, Co-Al [43] and Co-W-B [44] barriers for Cu metallization. The high concentration of W in $\mathrm { C o W _ { h } }$ promotes the diffusion of W atoms and the subsequent formation of tungsten oxide. This process, coupled with the high surface energy of 69 mJ $\mathbf { m } ^ { - 2 }$ , results in a moderate adhesion energy of 52.7 MPa. Note that. The data of Table 2 apparently suggest that the magnitude of the adhesion strength, along with the film’s hardness, is a key electromigration-mitigation factor, which in turn places the electromigration-reliability ranking of the four different Co deposits in decreasing order from $\mathrm { C o W _ { m } , C o W _ { h } , C o W _ { l } }$ to Co.

Here, the content of the W in Co is minor (0.03, 0.06 or 0.11 at.%), and thus the effective valence $Z ^ { * }$ , diffusivity D and electrical resistivity ρ of the alloyed Co are assumed to be the same as those of the unalloyed Co. Stressing the Co and W-added Co lines with an identical current density under the same temperature should induce the same electromigration flux at equilibrium according to Eq. (5). Thus, the reason for the W-added Co lines to yield a higher resistance to a variety of flux divergences showing a reduced void growth rate and extended electromigration lifetime, as implicitly confirmed by their smaller n factors, is related to the higher film mechanical properties. As stated, compressive and tensile stresses tend to build up, respectively, in the anode and cathode sides of a damaged region around the grain boundaries or material interfaces. The relaxation of the stress gradient by a back-diffusion process accelerates the formation and growth of the voids there [52]. The high adhesion strength and hardness of the W-added $\mathbf { C o } ,$ especially $\mathrm { C o W } _ { \mathrm { m } } ,$ contribute to the inhibition of stress relaxation during electromigration stressing, thus mitigating electromigration and prolonging interconnect’s lifetime. A thin polycrystalline conductive film with a higher adhesion strength and hardness would have a stronger substrate’s binding force and a tighter (or tougher) grain structure, which would put it more resistant to electromigration voiding or thermal stressing [53, 54]. Indeed, the SEM micrographs in Fig. 3 show that the thermal stability of the Co film is worse than that of the $\mathrm { C o W _ { m } }$ film; the Co interconnect line also has an inferior electromigration reliability, as compared to all W-added Co interconnect lines.

The STEM-HAADF image of the unalloyed Co line (Fig. 7c) exhibits a ‘clean, smooth’ contour, suggesting a relatively low defect density; the line also gives a ‘perfect’ lattice fringe image (Fig. 7d) and [0001] zoneaxis Fourier transform pattern of HCP-Co (inset, Fig. 7d). By contrast, the $\mathrm { C o W _ { m } }$ line comprises a stacking of equiaxed grains (Fig. 7b), seemingly offering a more complicated grain structure that could inhibit grain-boundary electromigration. Moreover, the $\mathrm { C o W _ { m } }$ line exhibits an HAADF image with an intricate, rough contour (Fig. 7e), suggesting a relatively high defect density. Its high-resolution TEM image (Fig. 7f), taken along the [0001] zone axis, clearly shows the existence of stacking faults on (0001) basal planes, associated with a streaky diffraction pattern of HCP-Co (inset of Fig. 7f). Comparing the unalloyed $\mathbf { C o } ,$ the equiaxed $\mathrm { C o W _ { m } }$ has a more complex grain structure and a higher density of immobile planar defects, which would offer a maze of diffusion routes to retard the void-growth rate.

In sum, the mitigation of Co electromigration by the alloying of extremely diluted W is directly related to an improvement of the film’s mechanical properties and a reduction in the film’s surface energy. Grain-structure refinement also plays a role in the reliability reinforcement.

surface_text: An all-wet SAM-seeding and electroless-plating process has been developed to form thin films of Co and extremely diluted CoW alloys with controlled thin-film properties, including deposition rates, alloy compositions, deposit surface morphologies and microstructure stability against thermal stressing. We then extend this all-wet process to fill these metal films into SiO<sub>2</sub> trenches, eventually fabricating nanolines of three different CoW alloys for electromigration-behavior evaluations, using nanolines of Co as a reference. The electromigration mitigation for all three nanolines of Co alloys with 0.03 at.%, 0.06 at.% and 0.11 at.% of added W, termed $\mathrm { C o W _ { l } , C o W _ { m } }$ and $\mathrm { C o W _ { h } } ,$ respectively, under accelerated current stressing conditions of the order of $1 0 ^ { 7 } \mathrm { A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ has been confirmed. Most noticeably, the $\mathrm { C o W _ { m } }$ line containing a moderate amount of W, while only 0.06 at.%, yields a significantly reduced current density scaling factor of 0.33, which is much smaller than that of the Co line (0.50). So, it also yields a much slower void growth rate, associated with an electromigration lifetime at least twice as long as that of the Co line. While a variety of advanced TEM analyses fail to locate the trace amount of W which is less than one atom in about 1000 cobaltmatrix atoms, the 0.06 at% added W markedly elevates the adhesion strength and hardness of Co from 35.8 to 56.1 MPa and 14.8 to 17.5 μN $\mathrm { n m } ^ { - 1 } ,$ respectively. Moreover, it also reduces Co surface energy from 70 to 60 mJ $\mathbf { m } ^ { - 2 }$ , favoring the wetting of the electroless deposits onto the underlying substrate. A fourth benefit given by the optimum W content, as found from advanced STEM/TEM analysis, is that the big electromigration-accelerating blocking grains, as exist in the Co line, are absent from the $\mathrm { C o W _ { m } }$ line. The full account of the thin-film properties being investigated correlates well with the reliability performance of the four different metallic thin films/interconnects under thermal/electricfield stressing. It also reasonably explains why the ranking of their electromigration reliability being increased from $\mathbf { C o } ,$ CoW (0.03 at.%), $\mathrm { C o W _ { h } }$ (0.11 at.%) to $\mathrm { C o W _ { m } }$ (0.06 at.%).

In electroless plating, both ultrasonication and stirring serve the same overall purpose, which is to ensure a uniform and high-quality metal deposition on the surface of the object being plated. Ultrasonication uses high-frequency sound waves to create microscopic vibrations in the solution to dislodge gas bubbles and enhance mass transfer [82]. In electroless Co-P plating, particularly in solutions with low cobalt sulfate concentration as fewer cobalt ions available, the diffusion process becomes more critical for maintaining a steady supply of ions to the substrate surface. The ability of ultrasonication to improve diffusion has a greater impact on accelerating the deposition rate in such scenarios [64]. Ultrasound irradiation reduces the activation energy of the electroless deposition reaction. This essentially means the reaction requires less energy to occur, allowing for a comparable deposition rate at a lower temperature [83]. The mechanism behind this improvement is attributed to ultrasonic cavitation. The collapse of cavitation bubbles on the solid surface generates micro-jets which effectively clean the catalytic surface by removing contaminants leading to a larger active surface area for catalysis [84]. Yu et al. [85] found that at high ultrasonication power (100 W), the film exhibits cracks on the surface. This is likely because excessive agitation disrupts the film growth process, leading to weak bonding between the deposited particles and creating cracks. They recommend 90 W for deposition of relatively smaller and more regular shaped crystallites.

Magnetic properties ofelectroless Co films, particularly coercivity, have been extensively studied from the beginning. Coercivity is the ability of a ferromagnetic material to resist external magnetic field without being magnetized. Tuneable coercivity of electroless Co-P combined with ultra-thin nature of the deposited film makes it a candidate of interest for high density magnetic recording medium [8, 9, 78]. Ouchi et al. [125] fabricated CoNiP nanodot arrays shorter than 50 nm with high perpendicular magnetic coercivities, using electroless deposition process (Fig. 10a). This is a crucial property for perpendicular magnetic recording technology to increase storage density. Co-P films are promising for magnetic rotary encoders, enabling magnetization into 2048 magnetic pole pairs with uniform output [126]. This improves resolution and accuracy for angle and displacement measurements.

Electroless Co-P deposits typically have a fine-grained structure, which contributes to their low friction coefficients and good wear resistance. However, the wear and friction behavior of the deposit can be further improved by annealing the deposit at an elevated temperature. Annealing causes the metal grains to grow, which results in a more uniform and stronger deposit. Klingenberg et al. [127]reported the microhardness (VHN) of Co-B to be 716 kg-f/mm<sup>2</sup> and of Co-P to be 883 kg-f/mm<sup>2</sup> after heat treatment at 350 °C. Composite coating like Co-SiC can exhibit high hardness even without heat treatment [116]. Self-lubricating Co-WS film (Fig. 10b) with very low coefficient of friction can be produced via electroless route [115]. It is also reported that presence of cobalt in electroless film enhances corrosion resistance in acidic [128] and saline environment [14].

Electrolysis involves the decomposition of water into hydrogen and oxygen gases. The material of the electrodes can affect the rate of hydrogen and oxygen production. Noble metals (Ru and Pt) are often used due to their catalytic properties but they are expensive. Transition metal-based catalysts (Co–B[52], Co-Mo-B [53], Co-P [31, 129], Co-P-B [130] etc.) offer more economical options. Electroless deposition is explored as a promising method for achieving uniform and adherent catalyst layers on electrode surface. Catalytic activity of Co-P significantly depends on phosphorus content, with the coating containing 11 wt% P achieving optimal hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) performance, notably a low overpotential of 98.9 mV at 10 mA $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ [131]. Efficiency of Co-P-B catalysts stems from synergistic electronic interactions, where electron transfer from B to Co, often modulated by P, creates active sites and optimizes adsorption capabilities [132, 133]. Whether synthesized as coatings on Ni foam for enhanced hydrogen evolution from ammonia borane [132] and sodium borohydride hydrolysis [134], or as amorphous nanoparticles [133] for overall water splitting, Co-P-B materials demonstrate superior reaction rates, lower activation energies, and excellent stability, making them promising candidates for sustainable hydrogen production. Electron micrograph of Co-coated Ni foam developed for catalytic water splitting is shown in Fig. 10c.

Adding small percentage of micro or nano-sized ceramic particles $( \mathrm { A l } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 3 }$ , SiC, MgO, WC, etc.) to metals can make them stronger and tougher as the hard ceramic particles act like tiny obstacles, making it harder for the metal to deform or break. Poor wettability can be a problem in metal matrix composites. If the metal does not adhere well to the ceramic particles, the composite material will be weaker and more likely to fail. One way to improve wettability is to coat the ceramic particles with a different material. This coating can act as a bridge between the metal and the ceramic, making it easier for the metal matrix to spread out and cover the ceramic particles. In recent decades, cobalt is being proven to be a good choice for coating ceramic particles in metal matrix composites [70, 119, 120]. Nambiar et al. [139] successfully developed aluminum matrix composites reinforced with cobalt-coated carbon nanotubes and Al2024 powder, designed for aircraft and automotive applications. A crucial finding was that a 10 µm electroless cobalt coating thickness was essential for maintaining reinforcement integrity and preventing defects during fabrication, thereby enhancing composite properties for these uses.

surface_text: Diffusion barriers (Fig. 10f) are crucial in microelectronic devices to prevent unwanted interdiffusion of atoms between different materials, which can lead to device failure. Electroless Co-P [4, 5, 108], Co-W–P [86, 105, 155], and Co-W-B [50] can be employed as interfacial layer in microelectronic contacts to prevent the inter diffusion of materials such as copper [156] and lead-free solders [5], ensuring the long-term reliability of electronic devices. A minimal 0.1% addition of manganese oxide (MnO) particles to electroless Co also reportedly improves its resistance to electromigration by physically blocking atomic movement [157]. Electroless deposited Co-P-W films, particularly those with over 12% P and 2% W, serve as excellent barrier layers in structures like through-silicon vias [158]. Compared to chloride free Pd activation, a PdCl /HCl-based activation process is noted to yield superior, residue-free deposition for such Co-P-W capping layers [159].

Enhanced Deposition Rate and Bath Efficiency: A persistent challenge is the low deposition rate and bath efficiency. Future research should focus on novel reducing agents, catalysts, or additives to accelerate kinetics without compromising quality or stability.

Electroless cobalt plating is a versatile technique capable of depositing a wide range of cobalt-based coatings, including pure cobalt and various binary and ternary alloys such as Co-P, Co-B, Co–Ni-P, Co-W–P, and Co-W-B. By carefully adjusting the composition of the plating bath and operating conditions, it is possible to tailor the properties of the deposited coatings to meet specific application requirements. These coatings offer numerous advantages, including improved corrosion and wear resistance, enhanced magnetic information storage capabilities, ability to serve as effective barrier layers against copper diffusion or acting as a catalyst in H generation via electrolysis. While many potential applications have been explored, there is still significant room for further research and development in this area. This review aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the electroless cobalt plating process by serving as a valuable resource for information on the various chemical baths and operating conditions employed by previous researchers.

Thin film deposition technology is critical to realize high-quality cobalt interconnects. Physical vapor deposition [12,13] (PVD), chemical vapor deposition [14,15] (CVD), atomic layer deposition [16–18] (ALD), and electrodeposition [19–21] are the primary synthesis methods reported to date. PVD is a widely used film deposition technique, yet its filling efficiency and step coverage remain inadequate, primarily due to one-direction linear de position characteristics. This results in particles with large incidence angles failing to enter the trenches and instead depositing at the trench openings [22]. Consequently, the opening closes before the trench is fully filled [23]. To solve this problem, the industrial sector has de veloped specific PVD technologies, such as ionized PVD and collimated sputtering [24,25]. Nevertheless, the hole problem in small-sized channels still exists. In addition, CVD tech nologies have better filling capabilities, especially when trench widths are around several hundred nanometers, such as plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition [26]. ALD possesses the unique characteristic of layer-by-layer self-limiting growth, providing exceptional step coverage and film uniformity. However, its deposition rate is exceedingly low, making it particularly suitable for applications such as barrier layers and seed layers [27]. In contrast, electroplating technology is extensively utilized in damascene copper interconnect processes, where it enables bottom-up film growth and demonstrates remarkable filling capabilities [28,29]. During the electroplating process, precise control over parameters such as applied current, anode material, accelerants, inhibitors, planarization agents, and mass transport allows for the fine-tuning of deposition rate, grain size, morphology, impurity content, and stress [30]. This level of control highlights the considerable potential for further advancement of metal-interconnect trench-filling techniques.

surface_text: # Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation

The major mechanism of corrosion inhibition effect by nicotinic acid (NA) is to form a passivation film which adsorbs on cobalt (Co) surface so as to strengthen the surface impedance and isolate the corrosion medium. In an alkaline environment (pH 10), NA exists in the form of Nic<sup>2−</sup> ions, which are negatively charged. Driven by electrostatic forces and Van der Waals forces between NA molecule (N atom and the carboxyl) and cobalt atom, Nic<sup>2−</sup> ions are appealed to the Co(OH)<sub>2</sub>, leading to the appearance of Co(II)-NA molecule groups. NA molecules produce a single or multilayer self-assembled Co(II)-NA film on the cobalt surface and further preven the corrosion on Co film.
Keywords: Cobalt interconnection Nicotinic acid Corrosion inhibitor Electrochemistry Molecule simulation

Cobalt (Co) is the interconnect metal of integrated circuits with the feature size of 10 nm and below, and Co corrosion is the main problem in cobalt interconnect chemical mechanical polishing (CMP). The introduction of inhibitors is one of the most ideal approaches to reduce corrosion. In this work, useful insights into the corrosion inhibition performance of nicotinic acid (NA), a green inhibitor, on cobalt film in alkaline medium were investigated via electrochemical characterization, surface analysis, quantum chemical calculation, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation, as well as the adsorption mechanism at atomic level was explored. NA belongs to anodic erosion inhibitor and its inhibition efficiency reached a maximum of 86.65 % at the concentration of 80 mM pH 10, which was identified by the contact angle and potentiodynamic polarization (PDP) test. The elec trochemical impedance spectra (EIS) suggested that the surface resistance was enhanced to prevent corrosion. Free energy obtained from the Langmuir model indicates that NA molecules are physically and spontaneously adsorbed on cobalt surface. XPS results further confirmed this point, which reveals that NA exists in the form of Nic<sup>2−</sup> in alkaline solution and forms a $\mathrm { C o ( O H ) _ { 2 } ( N i c ^ { 2 - } ) }$ molecule group (Co(II)-NA) on Co surface. Additionally, quantum chemical calculations based on density function theory (DFT) have approved that C–N bond and carboxyl group are the active sites of NA molecule and form the most significant electrostatic adsorption force with cobalt atoms. Moreover, it can be inferred from MD simulations that NA molecules are spontaneously and physically adsorbed on the cobalt surface at a certain angle. In a word, NA manifests its effectiveness in corrosion inhibition of cobalt and will become a potential cobalt CMP inhibitor. The research methods and results of this paper are beneficial to the study of the adsorption characteristics and inhibition mechanism of inhibitors on the metal surface, and provide a theoretical basis for optimizing the composition of Co CMP slurry.

In recent years, the addition of corrosion inhibitors has been proved to be an effective measure to inhibit corrosion of metal materials [9 11]. Many studies show that organic inhibitor molecules containing elements such as C, N, and O are often more effective in corrosion prevention, among which benzotriazole (BTA) is a common inhibitor and has been broadly commercialized [12 14]. The corrosion inhibition effect of BTA was firstly reported by Cotton et al. [15], and since then researchers have carried out a lot of researches on BTA $[ 9 , 1 6 , 1 7 ]$ . However, some current studies reported that BTA has a poor inhibition effect on Co corrosion in corrosive medium. Yang et al. [7] characterized the surface morphology of Co in the solution containing BTA and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ by SEM, and concluded that BTA could not effectively reduce the pitting caused by $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ on Co surface. Similarly, Lei et al. [18] suggested that BTA is no longer applicable to Co CMP by means of surface morphology test. In addition, the toxicity of BTA also limits its application in CMP [19,20]. Therefore, scholars have been committed to developing green and effective corrosion inhibitors for Co CMP, such as organic acid and vi tamins [21–23].

Notably, nicotinic acid, which belongs to the B3 group of vitamins, is widely used as an intermediate in the synthesis of various pharmaceuticals and shows favorable potential in corrosion inhibition effect. Mohamed et al. [23] investigated the polishing behavior and defects of cobalt samples with an aqueous mixture of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ,$ oxalic acid (OA), and nicotinic acid at pH 10. The results show that the alkaline solution including 80 mM NA can broadly reduce the corrosion current of cobalt samples and galvanic erosion between cobalt and copper, proving that NA can operate as an inhibitor for Co film in $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ solution. He et al. [24] concluded that NA offers a composite layer on the cobalt surface, and prevents further Co corrosion, while a combination of 10 mM NA and 5 mM TAZ minimized Co-Cu corrosion as measured by zero resistance galvanometer. Although it is confirmed that NA possesses an inhibition effect on cobalt, further studies on NA, such as the interaction process between NA and $\mathrm { C o } ,$ the adsorption mechanism of NA on Co surface and so on, have not been reported. Studying the adsorption of corrosion inhibitor on the metal surface is of great significance to explore the corrosion inhibition mechanism. This work mainly studies the inhibitory effect of NA on cobalt corrosion in alkaline medium, as well as the formation and mechanism of [NA-Co] complex.

Studies on the performance of inhibitor molecules only by conventional chemical experiments and characteristic methods are inadequate. The rapid development of theoretical chemistry provides a more scientific explanation for its research. Molecular simulation is a crucial approach to study the molecular chemical activity of corrosion inhibitors from a microscopic perspective [25,27–29]. The adsorption mechanism between inhibitors and metal substrates can be intuitively characterized by molecular simulation technology. Ma et al. [26] probed the effect of potassium oleate (PO) as a viable corrosion inhibitor for Cu films in $\mathrm { E D T A  – H _ { 2 } O _ { 2 } }$ based solution through combining chemical experiment analysis with molecular simulation. Density functional theory and molecular dynamics approaches were applied to study the inhibition mechanism at the atom level of PO on Cu(111) substrate. Yin et al. [16] evaluated the corrosion inhibition of BTA and TAZ at the molecular level via comparing quantum chemical descriptors. Therefore, it is necessary to further study the quantum chemical properties of NA and micro adsorption mechanism of NA on Co surface.

Considering that NA is an inexpensive, green, and easily available organic inhibitor, it was introduced into the alkaline (pH 10) solution. The molecular structure of NA is shown in Fig. 1. Contact angle and PDP measurements were carried out to determine the optimal concentration of NA. The passive film of NA was investigated by EIS, and the reaction between Co and NA was explored by XPS. Density functional theory was employed to study the properties of NA molecule. Several chemical descriptors were calculated to reveal active sites of NA molecule and the electron transfer characteristics between NA and Co atoms, as well as MD simulation was conducted to study the adsorption configuration, adsorption stability and adsorption sites of NA on Co surface. This work provides a more in-depth insight into the development of alkaline cobalt CMP slurry.

The adsorption of organic molecules on the metal surface will change its hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity and alters the contact angle of metal surface, while fresh metal surfaces usually present hydrophilicity, hence the contact angle reflects the adsorption effect of the inhibitor [30]. Fig. 2 illustrates contact angle of cobalt samples treated with different concentrations of NA and compared with that treated with CA. After CA treatment, the natural oxide layer on the cobalt surface was removed, and the contact angle of the cobalt surface reduced from $5 5 ^ { \circ }$ to 47◦, obtaining the fresh cobalt surface [31]. The contact angle increased to $6 7 ^ { \circ }$ following 40 mM NA treatment and increased steadily with the increase of NA concentration until the maximum contact angle reached $8 3 ^ { \circ }$ when the concentration was 80 mM. When the concentrations of NA were 90 and 100 mM, the contact angles were 82◦ and 83◦, respectively, which remained basically unchanged compared with that of 80 mM. These results show that when the concentration of NA is greater than 80 mM, the adsorption of NA molecules on the cobalt surface reaches saturation.

According to the contact angle results, PDP tests were carried out to evaluate the effect of corrosion inhibition of NA with the concentration less than 100 mM on cobalt electrode. Fig. 3 shows the PDP curves of cobalt electrode treated with different NA concentrations.

With the introduction of NA, both the anode and cathode branches of Tafel curves have the tendency to extend to the region of low corrosion current density. Compared with the cathode branches, the corrosion current density of the anode branches differs from one another markedly, i.e. the reduction reaction rate of dissolved oxygen at the cathode basically remains unchanged, while the metal ionization process occurring at the anode is inhibited. Accordingly, nicotinic acid belongs to the anodic corrosion inhibitor. The linear region of anodic branch, named as passivation region, proves that NA molecules gradually adhere to the cobalt surface to form a protective film and reduce the corrosion degree. It is noteworthy that the slope at the end of the 40 mM NA anode branch (circled in red) sinks, which is caused by the incompactness of the passivation film as the local corrosion medium may interact with the metal through the protective layer to aggravate the metal ionization. The illustration in Fig. 3 shows the PDP test curves of cobalt electrode in NA solutions with concentrations of 80, 90 and 100 mM, respectively. It can be seen that these three curves almost coincide, which indicates the surface corrosion of Co electrode is similar.

Additionally, the corrosion inhibition efficiency $( \eta _ { \mathrm { T } } )$ calculated by Eq. (1) are also shown in Table 1.

When the concentration of NA exceeds 80 mM, the variations of $E _ { \mathrm { c o r r } }$ and $I _ { \mathrm { c o r r } }$ of cobalt electrode are very small, among which values of $E _ { \mathrm { c o r r } }$ are − 0.499 \~ − 0.461 V, and $I _ { \mathrm { c o r r } }$ is between $2 . 8 7 6 \times 1 0 ^ { - 1 }$ and $2 . 9 5 0 \times 1 0 ^ { - 1 } \mu \mathrm { A / c m ^ { 2 } }$ . And the corrosion in hibition efficiency stabilizes between 86 % and 87 %. This indicates that there is no significant difference in the corrosion state of cobalt electrode, i.e., the adsorption of NA on cobalt surface reaches saturation at 80 mM. When the concentration of NA is 80 mM, the minimum value of $I _ { c o r r } \mathrm { i s } 2 . 8 7 6 \times 1 0 ^ { - 1 } \mu \mathrm { A / c m } ^ { 2 } .$ and the $\eta _ { T }$ reaches the maximum of 86.65 %, suggesting that NA performs the optimal corrosion inhibitory effect at 80 mM.

The electrochemical experiment results are consistent with the contact angel test. It is reasonable to suppose that the tightest passive film is formed by 80 mM NA, so as to provide the strongest corrosion inhibition [24,33]. In order to understand the basic adsorption mode of NA on the cobalt/solution interface, several adsorption isotherm models were exploited. The results of PDP fitted show that the adsorption between NA and Co surfaces conforms to the Langmuir isotherm model suitably. The Langmuir isotherm equations are described by Eqs. (2) and (3)[31]:

EIS measurement was used to analyze the passivation effect of physically adsorbed protective film on cobalt surface in alkaline medium. Fig. 5(a) shows the Nyquist impedance spectra of the Co electrodes in different concentrations of NA, which can better understand the structure of passivation layer. Since the Nyquist curve is a 1/4 arc, the charge transfer controls the erosion on cobalt/alkaline medium interface, and the equivalent circuit is a simple model formed by electron exchange on passivation film. In the event that the general shape of the impedance spectra does not change with the introduction of inhibitors, the reaction principle of the corrosive medium could be considered as unaffected [35]. Meanwhile the radius of the spectrum increases with the increase of NA concentration, suggesting that the adsorption film turns to be more completed [36]. The radius of imped ance spectrum reaches the maximum when the concentration of NA is 80 mM, which is consistent with PDP results. Nonetheless, the center of the 1/4 arc is apparently below the x-axis, known as the frequency dispersion effect, which is on account of the non-ideal capacitive behavior of the cobalt/medium interface generated by the non-uniformity of cobalt electrode surface.

That is to say, the inhibition mechanism is the formation of an adsorption layer on the cobalt surface caused by NA, which enhances the surface resistance. And the enlargement of NA concentration enables the Co surface to attract more inhibitor molecules to possess a thicker and denser inhibition film.

XPS was introduced to confirm the chemical composition of cobalt samples to further analyze the reaction state of cobalt surface. The XPS spectra and corresponding Co 2p spectra of cobalt samples after being treated with CA and immersed in 80 mM NA are shown in Fig. 6. Fig. 6 (a) shows that the two curves have three distinct peaks (C, O, and Co). In contrast, the peak intensities of C, O, and Co soaked in NA are signifi cantly higher than that of soaked in citric acid. This phenomenon is consistent with the element of NA molecules, and it can be inferred that inhibitor NA and its relative products can successfully assemble on the cobalt surface, issuing in the change of peak intensity of homologous elements. In addition, the appearance of N peak on the Co sample’s surface is induced by the pyrazole ring in the NA molecule [32].

Frontier molecular orbital (FMO) theory has been widely applied in the field of chemical structure to evaluate the efficiency of inhibitors, as well as explore the mechanism of interaction between inhibitors and metal surfaces [42–44]. Hence, a series of quantum chemical parameters, such as the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) energy levels, and the energy gap (ΔE) were calculated by DFT method. Firstly, the structure of NA molecular was optimized, and then properties of the frontier orbital of NA molecule were evaluated.
Fig. 7. Corrosion inhibition schematic diagram of NA on cobalt surface.

Generally, the higher HOMO energy or a lower LUMO energy manifests a mightier capability of molecular electron pairs to transfer or vacant orbitals to accept electron pairs. For corrosion inhibitors, this also means a more violent trend of binding and adsorption with metal surface atoms, that is, more efficient corrosion inhibition competence [45]. On top of that, the molecule activity is strengthened with the decrease of ΔE $( \Delta E { = } \Delta E _ { L U M O } - \Delta E _ { H O M O } )$ , i.e. the reduction of ΔE promotes the impact of corrosion inhibition.

Fig. 8(a) and (b) demonstrate the optimized NA molecule and the electron cloud distribution of HOMO and LUMO. In the HOMO diagram, the electron cloud is mainly distributed on the $\mathrm { N } { = } \mathrm { C }$ bond, while the N––C bond and the carboxyl group (-COOH) occupy the primary electron cloud of LUMO, indicating that chemical reactivity exists in the $\mathrm { N } { = } \mathrm { C }$ bond and the -COOH. The truth that the value of ΔE for BTA $\left( \Delta E _ { B T A } { = } 3 . 7 9 7 \ \mathrm { e V } \right)$ [8] is larger than that of NA $( \Delta E _ { N A } { = } 2 . 1 1 4 \ \mathrm { e V } )$ signifies that the corrosion inhibition performance of NA surpasses that of BTA. Electrostatic potential (ESP) results can further confirm this conclusion, as shown in Fig. 8(c). The region of electrophilic with the highest negative potential is marked in red, while the blue region indicates nucleophilic. As shown in Fig. 8(d), the highest red region is located on N6 and O8, as well as the blue region covers the H14 atom, which fully suggests that the functional sites of NA on the cobalt surface are N––C bond and the carboxyl group.

MD simulation can visualize the interaction status between the in hibitor molecule and metal surface [6]. Fig. 9(a) shows the most steady configuration of NA on the surface of Co(111), that the NA molecule is adsorbed at a certain angle on the Co surface. It is generally assumed that the adsorption process of corrosion inhibitor molecules on the metal surface turns to be more settled and solid with the accumulation of negative adsorption energy. The $E _ { a d s }$ value is − 24.382 kJ/mol, indicating that the NA molecules can be spontaneously and equably adsorbed on the Co surface.

The radial distribution function (RDF) is a common parameter to estimate the connection length, which can reflect the chemical bonds after the interaction between the inhibitor and metal surface [52]. Actually, RDF is the ratio of the local density around a particle to the bulk density of the system in a given coordinate. The local density near the target particle (small r value) is different from the bulk density of the system, but the local density should be the same as the bulk density when it is far away from the target particle, i.e. when the value of r is large, the value of RDF should be close to 1 [53]. In this work, we focused on nicotinic acid as a potential corrosion inhibitor for cobalt CMP in alkaline medium, and the adsorption behavior of NA was systematically revealed by several characteristic techniques and molecular simulations. The results of contact angel and electrochemical test show that corrosion efficiency reached the maximum value of 86.65 % at the concentration of 80 mM. The adsorption of NA on cobalt surface follows the Langmuir adsorption isotherm, which is a spontaneous physical process. EIS further suggests that with the increase of NA concentration, the passivation film covered on cobalt surface became more complete, resulting in the increase of surface resistance. According to the results of XPS, NA molecules exist in the form of $\mathrm { N i c } ^ { 2 - }$ ions in alkaline environment, and physically assemble on $\mathrm { C o ( O H ) _ { 2 } }$ to form Co(II)-NA molecular groups to isolate the permeation of corrosive medium. DFT calculation and MD simulation indicate that NA molecule is adsorbed on the Co(111) surface at a certain angle through Coulomb force and van der Waals force, which are derived from the interaction of $\mathrm { N } { = } \mathrm { C }$ bond and carboxyl in NA molecule and surface cobalt atoms. The results of this work on passive film of NA on Co surface and its microscopic properties provide a theoretical basis for optimizing the composition of Co CMP slurry, and also provide support for subsequent researches of exploring synergistic effect of NA and other slurry components. In conclusion, NA is suggested to be an effective potential inhibitor for Co CMP in IC manufacturing process. Its physical adsorption on cobalt surface will help to improve the inhibitor removal effect in post CMP cleaning.

With the continuous development of chips towards high integration, the chip interconnect size is constantly decreasing and copper interconnect technology faces huge challenges. When the interconnect size is reduced to below 7 nm, copper wire conducts exponential growth in resistivity due to its grain boundary scattering [1, 2], leading to chip overheating and increased power consumption, which in turn affects the computing speed and overall device performance [3]. On the other hand, copper interconnects require a barrier layer of approximately 2 nm tantalum nitride (TaN) to prevent copper metal from diffusing into the silicon dielectric layer, thus further increasing the interconnect resistance [4]. Metal cobalt has the advantages of short electron mean free path, resistance to electromigration and good compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing, which has been considered as a new type of interconnect material to replace copper [5–7]. Currently, the pioneer manufacturers such as Intel and TSMC are also proposing to adopt cobalt as a new interconnect metal for advanced chip manufacturing [8]. At present, the cobalt interconnects in silicon chip are realized through electroplating cobalt super-filling. Although there have been reports on the research of electroplated cobalt super-filling in chip microholes [9–11], compared with electrodeposited copper, electrodeposited cobalt is prone to forming holes and cracks due to such issues as hydrogen evolution, homogenization and poor coating quality [12]. Electroless plating is one of the most practical routs to realize cobalt plating in industrial-scale since it presents a good coverage ability, facile processing and low cost. Particularly, additives play a crucial role in electroless plating [13–16]. The appropriate additives not only can improve the quality of the chemical coating, but also enhance its properties such as density, corrosion resistance, wear resistance, and conductivity.

Saccharin (SAC) is a common organic, non-toxic small molecule that can be used as an additive in the electroplating process to improve the quality of coatings, reduce internal stress, refine grains, enhance the glossiness and reflectivity of coatings [17–19]. Altamirano-Garcia et al. [20] studied the effects of sulfates, chlorides, and saccharin on the electrodeposition of cobalt nickel alloys, and found that the addition of saccharin significantly improved the deposition current efficiency and suppressed hydrogen production, thereby improving the density of the alloy coating. Hoghoghifard et al. successfully improved the microwave absorption performance of nickel coated fabrics by adding saccharin to the plating solution [21]. They found that adding saccharin can reduce surface resistivity, refine grain size, enhance hysteresis loss, and ultimately improve the microwave shielding effect of the fabric. Kolonits et al. found that adding saccharin can significantly refine grain size, increase lattice defect density, and thus improve the hardness of nickel films [22]. Currently, researchers explored the additive mechanism through molecular dynamics simulations and calculations of quantum chemistry, which can effectively resolve molecular-metal interactions [23, 24]. Nevertheless, the researches on quantum chemical calculation of the electroless cobalt plating under the influence of additives are insufficient. Therefore, it is of great significance to establish a method based on quantum chemical calculation to study the effect of additives on cobalt plating.

Due to the presences of both sulfonic acid groups (–SO H) and aldehyde groups in saccharin, the electron cloud density at certain positions of the benzene ring is relatively reduced. In the process of electroless cobalt plating, cobalt ions need to be reduced at sites with electron donating properties. Therefore, the adsorption of saccharin molecules on the cobalt surface hinders the continuous growth of cobalt at the c-site during the stacking process (Fig. 5c and Fig. 6c), leading to the formation of ab stacking and HCP cobalt texture. ## 3.1. Inhibition and maximum ofPVP inhibition

The inhibitive behavior of PVP in the solution was investigated through electrochemical measurements. Fig. 1 shows the significant decrease of cobalt stripping area and hysteretic voltammetric features in the solution with PVP. The current density decreases sharply in the presence of PVP (Fig. 1a). For example, after adding 5 mg/L PVP into plating solution, the stripping peak current density decreases from $2 1 \mathrm { m A } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ to $1 2 { \mathrm { m A } } / { \mathrm { c m } } ^ { 2 } .$ . In the meantime, the oxidation peak potential is also shifted negatively by 80 mV (from 0.36 V to 0.44 V vs Hg/ $\mathrm { H g } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 } ) .$ The change in stripping peak current density and oxidation peak potential both reveal that cobalt electrodeposition is inhibited by

PVP. The CV plot in Fig. 1b highlights that the cobalt deposition potential is negative correlated with the concentration of PVP which shows an enhancing effect on the polarization of cobalt electroplating. In addition, with the increasing concentration of PVP, cobalt electrodepositing was further inhibited, which is supported by the decreasing area of oxidation peaks.

The maximum state of PVP suppression was further studied. As is shown in Fig. 1c, the oxidation peak area of CV was calculated to illustrate the inhibition effect of PVP with different concentrations. The integral of the cobalt stripping peak area is defined as $\mathrm { Q } _ { 0 }$ without PVP and as Q with PVP, respectively [28]. The curve which displays the value of $\mathrm { Q } / \mathrm { Q } _ { 0 }$ as a function of the concentration of PVP can be divided into three stages (Fig. 1d). $\mathrm { Q } / \mathrm { Q } _ { 0 }$ values undergo a sharp drop with low concentration of PVP and a steady stage with the high concentration of PVP. Notably, an intermediate slope appears in the curve for the PVP concentration range between 15 mg/L and 81 mg/L. When the PVP concentration continues to increase to more than 81 mg/L, the inhibition of PVP in cobalt electroplating reaches maximum.

As well known, chloride ions could affect the quality of metal coating and influence the mechanisms of additives in metal electroplating bath [29, 30]. The impact of Cl in the PVP-involved electroplating system was analyzed through voltammetry curves (Fig. 2a). In contrast with the curves in Fig. 1a-b, the stripping peak current density decreases more sharply when 5 mg/L PVP was added into the solution. These results in CV curve imply that PVP can inhibit the electrodeposi tion of cobalt in both chloride-containing and non-chloride ion plating solutions. However, in the solution with Cl, less amount of PVP is needed to reach the saturation (Fig. 2b). As for the $\mathrm { Q } / \mathrm { Q } _ { 0 }$ value, this ratio decreases with increasing concentration of PVP and process is divided into two stages (Fig. 2b). The phenomenon of first stage that $\mathrm { Q } / \mathrm { Q } _ { 0 }$ values decrease sharply with adding PVP can be observed when the concentration of PVP is less than 10.65 mg/L. In the second stage, Q/Q values maintain relatively stable with further increased PVP concentration. In the absence of Cl (Fig. 1d), PVP in plating solution reaches the saturation at a much higher concentration. Furthermore, when 10 mg/L PVP was added, the oxidation peak area in solution with Cl $( \mathrm { Q } / \mathrm { Q } _ { 0 }$ value decreases from 1.0 to 0.42 in Fig. 2b) decreased more than the chlorine-free solution $( \mathrm { Q } / \mathrm { Q } _ { 0 }$ value decreases from 1.0 to 0.51 in Fig. 1d). It is indicated that PVP is a suppressant of electrodeposited cobalt which can negatively shifts the deposition potential of cobalt, and chloride ion helps to accelerate the suppression effect of PVP.

The increase of overpotential is attributed to the adsorption of PVP on the surface of cobalt. The reverse scan exhibits an obvious hysteresis in the solution with only 100 mg/L PVP (Fig. 2c), revealing an adsorption and re-adsorption process of PVP. After adding Cl into PVP solution, the CV curve in Fig. 2c displays a weaker hysteresis effect. Thus, the adsorption strength of PVP is enhanced and Cl makes the adsorption more stable. Fig. 2c also shows the synergistic effect between PVP molecules and chloride ions. Chlorine ions were added to the solution containing 100 mg/L PVP, and the absolute value of current density continued to decrease.

The molecular frontier orbital theory suggests that the key of chemical reactions is the HOMO and LUMO of the molecules [20]. The distribution of HOMO and LUMO of PVP was simulated by molecular orbital method (Fig. 3). The HOMO value $\left( \mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { H O M O } } \right)$ of a molecule determines its ability to lose electrons outward, and the LUMO value $\left( \mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { L U M O } } \right)$ represents its ability to accept electrons. Higher E and lower $\mathtt { E } _ { \mathrm { L U M O } }$ partly reflect the reactivity of molecule [32]. The $\mathtt { E _ { H O M O } }$ value of PVP is 6.877 eV (Fig. 3e), compared with 7.338 eV of PEG [21], indicating that PVP has relatively stronger electron donating ability. The simulated values imply that PVP is more likely to interact with cobalt cations and have an impact on electrodeposition of cobalt. Fig. 3e shows that the nitrogen element and oxygen element of the amide group are the main contributors to the HOMO orbital, which acts as the main electrophilic attack region. The organics with higher value of $\mathtt { E _ { H O M O } }$ tent to have stronger electron donating ability to bond with the d-orbital of the metal. PVP with amide group may bond with cobalt, facilitates formation of PVP adsorption and inhibits cobalt electroplating. The electrostatic potential distribution on the surface of molecular van der Waals force of PVP is displayed in Fig. 3a, which is widely used to predict molecular electron donating ability, electro-accepting ability and electrophilic reaction sites [33]. Areas with low ESP value are the positions of high electron density, which are considered to be more affinitive to the cobalt surface [34, 35]. PVP has lowest ESP value of 131.3 kJ/mol compared with PEG [21] ( 131.6 kJ/mol) (Fig. 3a). The electron density map shows that the carbonyl of the amide group contributes greatly to the electron donating ability of PVP. The amide group probably acts as reaction sites in the electrodeposition reaction by the quantum chemical calculations.

Convection have significant influence on the process of electrodeposition. For the electroplating with rotating electrodes, the higher rotating speed of electrode leads to the greater convection in the solution. PVP can effectively inhibit the electrodeposition of cobalt in strong convection because the potential was quickly reduced by 160 mV when 5 mg/L PVP was added in strong convection (2000 rpm) (Fig. 3c). However, when 5 mg/L of PVP was added at low rotating speed (200 rpm), the potential was reduced by 100 mV and the inhibitory effect was slowly balanced after 2000s. Ji et al. found that electrolyte flow plays an important role in electroplating process [36]. The convection intensity of the solution inside the hole is lower than the one outside. The local convection affects the transport boundary layer in cobalt electroplating. As a result, more PVP molecules are be transmitted from solution to the electrode surface per unit time in strong convection. In Fig. 3c, PVP demonstrates a faster suppression in the strong convective condition, which is conducive to filling holes in electroplating. PVP molecules can be adsorbed on surface faster, resulting in different concentration distribution of additives at surface and bottom of trenches at the initial stage of electrodeposition. The cause of the secondary current density distribution is the concentration gradient of the additive [37,38]. In addition, the electroplating experiment was also conducted. As shown in Fig. 3d, the silicon trench is sealed in cobalt electroplating without inhibitor during the process of cobalt electroplating which is consistent with the above discussion.

Cobalt filling was achieved in silicon trenches, which confirms that PVP is capable of being an inhibitor in the electrodeposited cobalt filling. The silicon-based chip has a series of trenches in which a layer of gold was sputtered and the recess was filled by electrodepositing cobalt (Fig. 4). Fig. 4d is a cross-sectional slice of the electrodeposited cobalt-filled silicon trench with full cobalt super-filling. In this work, cobalt super-filling is achieved in silicon trench with the addition of 100 mg/L PVP. It is assumed that PVP molecules adsorb rapidly on the plated surface in the presence of Cl.

Cobalt bottom up filling mechanism is proposed in Fig. 5. In the initial stage of electrodeposition, PVP molecules were quickly adsorbed on the surface, strongly inhibiting the growth of cobalt on the surface. Therefore, the deposition rate at the bottom is greater than that at the surface. Diffusional limitation and CDA of PVP long chain molecule both contribute to the higher deposition rate at the bottom than the one at the surface of the trench and obvious bottomup filling is then expected.

The effect of PVP involved in the electrodeposition of cobalt was further investigated by the characterization of morphology. PVP demonstrates considerable effect on electrodeposited cobalt crystals. The XRD results in Fig. 6a indicate that PVP inhibits the cobalt electrodeposition by affecting the growth of cobalt specific crystal surfaces. The electrodeposited cobalt mainly forms cubic crystals in Fig. 6a. And, it is worth mentioning that PVP reduced the intensity of diffraction peak of cobalt along the direction of 220, indicating that the introduction of PVP inhibited the growth of 220 surface of cobalt without affecting the growth of other crystal planes.

The contact angle test indicates that PVP can improve the wettability of plating solution effectively. As is shown in Fig. 6c-d, the contact angle of the plating solution without PVP is more than $3 0 ^ { \circ }$ on the cobalt surface and is reduced to 15° after adding 100 mg/L PVP. Better wettability of the solution enables more hydrogen to be released in time [39] and enhances coating quality in cobalt electrodeposition. PVP can also be used as surfactant in electrodeposited cobalt because the amide group and carbon chains of PVP can act as polar hydrophilic and hydrophobic group respectively. Meanwhile, according to the theory of electro-capillary, polarization can reduce the surface tension and contributes to the desorption of hydrogen, which is consistent with the discussion above.

In addition, PVP can refine particles and makes the cobalt layer more compact. The SEM images of electrodeposited cobalt in the solution without PVP display different particle size and roughness of surface without inhibitor (Fig. 6e). Fig. 6f shows the SEM of electrodeposited cobalt layer after adding 100 mg/L PVP and the surface morphology of the coating changed obviously in contrast with the one without PVP.

The uniformity of the coating was clearly improved by 3D roughness tests (Fig. 6g-h), and cobalt surface becomes more compact. Sa represents the arithmetic mean of the height values of all the peaks and troughs on plane A in Fig. 6g and Fig. 6h. The larger the value of Sa, the greater roughness of metal surface. The Sa value of electrodeposited cobalt layer in the solution without PVP is less than the Sa value of cobalt layer with 100 mg/L PVP in the electroplating solution, validating that PVP can improve the uniformity of cobalt layer in cobalt electrodeposition. In summary, PVP is an effective cobalt electrodeposition inhibitor. Besides, PVP can effectively facilitate hydrogen desorption, affect the surface morphology, and improve surface uniformity of cobalt layer.

Cobalt electroplating has great application potential in the fabrication of interconnection in electronic devices. More types of additives with the function of manipulating cobalt deposition rate and improving deposition quality of cobalt layer will be attempted in the following research.
